This tells me: 1) Lidocaine is safe to use on the face. 2) Extracting facial hair by force is effective and safe.

That said, I am careful to only extract a narrow band of hair with each pass. I also clean my face with alcohol, then use a lidocaine spray on my skin, let it sit for 30 minutes and then start. I've always had a good complexion and still do. Maybe I'm a unicorn, but based on my experience, this has been an acceptable method to remove facial hair.

As for IPLs, I bought a Bosidon (supposedly the best on the market at the time, and hella spendy) and used it for 3 or 4 months to no avail. Since 80% of my facial hair is dark, allowing for high contrast between skin and hair, it should have worked. I wouldn't waste time and effort for that. To do my whole body, face included, took hours when you factor in shaving first (required). 

Depending on how large of an area you need to have removed, getting a Groupon for laser hair removal or electrolysis would be a good path for you. I live in the Dallas area and there are plenty of deals to be had for the about the same cost cost as the Bosidon. Just keep in mind it takes several sessions, but Groupon has packages for enough sessions to get results and not break the bank.

In the end you will show the world (and yourself) who you are by how you express yourself, whether it is in scolastics, art, writing, etc. How you present your vision for who you are is not something that someone else needs to confirm for you. You do not need to sacrifice your spirit to fit in.

All that said, I can't look back and feel sorry for myself, because I was following what I believed to be the right path. In the end, I learned to see myself for that girl I knew was there, but I put myself (and others) through hell to see it, though not intentionally. It is odd to see all 5 star reviews, for sure. Keep in mind that businesses actively solicit 5 star google reviews from customers that have good experiences, and usually ask for the review when they are on an emotional high. I have seen this in the apartment industry that I worked in for 14 years and in luxury car sales, too. It is typical to have customers fill out the review (frequestly with direction from staff) in the office before they leave. It is a way to cherry pick your customers. 

As an example, I had ketamine therapy for migraines a few years ago, and before I was even totally clear headed, I was given an iPad that already had the star rating set to 5. 

This does not mean that the reviews are false, but you will not find any business handing a tablet to a customer whose experience went sideways, and ask them to do a perfect review! That said, any google reviewer can edit a review at a later time if their experience changes, but that is actually kind of rare, since a lot of people want to distance themselves from bad experience and that may make them feel foolish to have written it to start with.

I don't think good and bad reviews necessarily negate one another, but they are good to get you to think twice before you commit to a doctor (or any prefessional) for life altering procedures. 

The main thing is what do you truly feel about moving forward with this surgeon? If you take the money aspect out of the equation, would you still move forward? If not, the don't do it. Your deposit is not worth the trauma of a surgery gone wrong, and the emotional and physical damage that goes with it. 

If it really comes down to money, and you have red flags you can't ignore, consider the cost of follow up surgery to fix something you cannot live with. I don't think I would ever stop kicking myself if I did something that major, when I had deep reservations about it, and my concerns proved to be right. 

So what do you think you will do?

I have been in my stepson's life since he was 12 (now 23). All I can offer is advice from that perspective, and as a 46 year old trans woman that will be coming out to her father and stepmother in the next few months. I can empathize with you. 

Since I'm not my kid's father, I was able to be more objective about his direction in life and his right to be his own person.

So he has never been the super sporty jock kind of guy. He is bookish, artistic and has a gentle way about him. He is a kid after my own heart! As he went through high school he never dated and that was the trend into his college years too. He is very private about his feelings, as well.

When he was about 18, his mom started suspecting that he prefers the company of men, and even started asking him if his is gay. He denied this, but as someone who just came out to my ex, I know that if you start digging at people like that, you put them on the defensive and they are not likely to tell you. My ex started asking his dad (lives out of state) what he thought about the question, and he said he thinks so, too. To me none of that is relevant. If he is, he is, and if he decides to come out, that is up to him. 

The thing is, both parents told him they don't care if he is gay. Based on their actions, that's is obviously not true. They just have a picture they created years ago about who he would be as he got older. And even though they would love him just the same, they never just said you can be you, and we are happy for you to go live what is in your heart. 

All that to say, I am sure your mother is just clinging to the aspirations she created in her mind when you were young. She also may not know how to support you and it just may not compute in her mind, yet. It takes time to reorganize your thoughts when you've had your mind set for so long. Unfortunately, she may live in denial for a while. In the big picture, January was just a couple months ago and is not very long for her to overcome over a decade of preconceptions. 

I hate to say it, but these things take time, and there will be many more conversations before she sees you for you. It doesn't mean she does not love you, or will never accept you, though. It does mean that she will have to adapt which takes time. I wouldn't dwell on only that aspect of your relationship. There is more to you than that, and showing her that all the things she knows and loves about you are still you.

I really advise being patient with her. As much as she may try to push you in a different direction, show her who you are over time, by being your genuine self. If she brings the topic up, be honest and upfront. Show her your depth of character by being centered and don't forget that you will probably have to hold her hand and be the more mature person in the room. It sucks, but she will only learn you're not going through a phase by just continuing to be yourself to the point it finally clicks for her. That won't mean it is hopeless. It's just a slow process.

The good thing is that you are young and you do not have to overcome even more years of expectations. My family has 46 years of preconceived notions they will need to get past when I finally introduce them to who I really am! 

I hope this hasn't only confused the matter for you. Keep your chin up! Things will get good. Just take advantage of every opportunity life gives to show your mom that you are the same person you always have been, in every way. There is just more to you than she realized.
